When I compare two software suppliers, I never start with the price on the page. Pricing pages are written to make every product look cheap. One supplier charges per seat, whereas the other charges per transaction, so the two numbers mean nothing side by side. The first thing I do is build one scenario: our number of users, our volume, and three years, not one. Then I look for the hidden costs. Is the connector included, or is it an add-on? Is there a setup fee? Is storage free? And finally, I ask both suppliers for a flat fee for the first year. The supplier that answers clearly, without changing the subject, usually wins. The cheapest page almost never does.

Last year a customer sent me a competitor's pricing page with one line: they are thirty percent cheaper. My first reaction was to offer a discount. I didn't. Instead, I asked for one hour to build a comparison on the same basis. Their price was usage-based, while ours was per seat. With the customer's real volume, they were cheaper in the first year. However, by the third year they were twenty percent more expensive. I sent a one-page table, with one difference per line and one sentence under each line. No adjectives, just numbers. The customer called me the next day and said: thank you, nobody explained it like that. We signed at our price. The discount was never discussed again.
